case_info.scenario: A previously healthy 55-year-old man presented to his local family medicine clinic after waking up with a buzzing sensation in his chest. He denied chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations, lightheadedness, diaphoresis, fever, lower-extremity edema, or fatigue. He worked in retail sales and had been lifting televisions in the preceding days. His initial vital signs included blood pressure of 124/71 mm Hg, pulse of 100 beats/min, temperature of 36.6 °C, respiratory rate of 18 breaths/min, oxygen saturation of 98% as measured by pulse oximetry, and body mass index (calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared) of 25. He was directed to the local emergency department. On physical examination, he was alert, oriented, and in no acute distress. Chest palpation demonstrated a thrill along the sternal border, and the point of maximal impulse was laterally displaced. Auscultation revealed regular rate and rhythm, with normal first (S1) and soft second (S2) heart sounds. A buzzing, decrescendo, grade 6/6 diastolic murmur (DM) was heard at the right upper sternal border (Figure 1;Video 1). The murmur radiated throughout the precordium, into the abdomen, and to the bilateral carotids and was audible in the posterior thorax. Electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm, moderate voltage criteria for left ventricular (LV) hypertrophy, and ST and T abnormalities in the lateral leads.

case_info.explanation: D. Perform transthoracic echocardiography in the emergency department The clinical presentation of symptoms with a grade 6 DM strongly suggests severe underlying structural pathology requiring urgent investigation. Severe aortic valve regurgitation (AR) or a ruptured sinus of Valsalva aneurysm should be suspected. AR results in a decrescendo DM along the sternal border and can be distinguished from mitral stenosis based on its qualities and location. The differential diagnosis of a DM also includes patent ductus arteriosus, although this would be expected to result in a continuous (systolic and diastolic) murmur enveloping the second heart sound. Avoiding lifting, initiating β-blockers, and routine follow-up underestimate the risk of sudden decompensation related to severe underlying structural cardiac pathology. Although endocarditis can result in destructive valvular changes, the patient’s lack of fever and systemic symptoms do not support this diagnosis. History is not suggestive of an acute coronary syndrome requiring serial troponins. While chest computed tomographic (CT) angiography would provide anatomic definition of the aortic valve and root, it would not provide real-time hemodynamic assessment, which is the key next step to understand the patient’s loud murmur. Transthoracic echocardiogram confirmed severe valvular AR with holodiastolic flow reversal in the abdominal aorta (Figure 2). The aortic valve was tricuspid without apparent prolapse or flail (Video 2). The sinus of Valsalva was severely enlarged (55-mm diameter), with mild enlargement of the ascending aorta (42-mm diameter). LV chamber size was moderately to severely enlarged (end-diastolic dimension, 63 mm; end-systolic dimension, 40 mm; LV mass, 285 g). Gated chest CT angiography (Figure 2) confirmed a severely dilated aortic root (sinuses of Valsalva dimensions, 59 × 57 × 54 mm) without dissection. The coronary arteries were well visualized and without atherosclerosis. The left anterior descending and left circumflex coronary arteries had separate ostia. LV enlargement was confirmed. Urgent cardiac surgical evaluation was arranged given the aortic root size and severe AR. The LV enlargement implied that the AR was chronic, possibly acutely worsened by recent lifting. Surgical intervention with hypothermic circulatory arrest was pursued. Intraoperatively, the aorta was friable, was asymmetric with a large noncoronary sinus, and had a severely dilated root. All cusps demonstrated deep fenestrations and fibrotic changes. An acute-appearing tear in the support of the right coronary cusp from the right-posterior commissure was noted (Figure 2). Bentall root placement with a 25-mm On-X mechanical valve (Artivion) and ascending aorta hemiarch repair with a 26-mm Dacron graft were performed. Transesophageal echocardiography on separation from cardiopulmonary bypass was normal. In this case, identification of grade 6 DM led to expedited evaluation, demonstrating how murmur characteristics can guide initial clinical decision-making. DMs are almost always indicative of pathological conditions. The presence of a DM is very useful in AR diagnosis, with a positive likelihood ratio of 8.8 and a negative likelihood ratio of 0.2 to 0.3.1 Grade 6 murmurs are rare and almost always systolic. The literature is scarce for grade 6 DMs, limited to a single patient with pulmonary regurgitation.2Murmur intensity can be crudely correlated with the severity of the regurgitant lesion, although the association is not linear as flow across large orifices can become more laminar.3Fluttering of the torn aortic cusp with turbulent flow may explain the vibratory or buzzing sensation the patient perceived. In this case, the severe nature of the AR, the fluttering torn cusp, and the patient’s thin chest wall likely contributed to the intensity of the DM. The patient was discharged on postoperative day 5. At 20-month clinical follow-up, he was asymptomatic with a normally functional aortic valve prosthesis.

[AI Assistant]: Excellent plan. Reviewing the recent coronary angiography to ensure stent patency is a standard and prudent step before proceeding with CRT device placement. Given the compelling physiological link, this should successfully address her dyssynchrony-induced MR and symptoms.

Case:
A 50-year-old woman presented to the dermatology department with a 10-year history of recurrent plaque outbreaks between her toes. She had a history of Bowen disease in the anus that had been treated with excision and skin grafting. Physical examination revealed multiple dark brown, flat, hyperproliferative lesions with ulcerations and erosions located between the toes and on the vulva (Figure 1). Additionally, a 5 × 4 × 1-cm ulcerated perianal tumor with easy bleeding was noted. Coagulation, thyroid, liver, and kidney test results were within the normal ranges. Tests for syphilis, HIV, and autoantibodies were negative. However, the foot lesions were positive for human papillomavirus (HPV) 16, and the perianal, vulvar, and cervical lesions were positive for HPV-6, HPV-16, and HPV-18. A complete blood cell count revealed a decreased lymphocyte count of 400/μL (range, 1100-3200/μL; to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001). The T-cell subset panel showed a total lymphocyte count of 564.45 cells/mL (range, 1200-3400 cells/mL) and a CD4+T-cell count of 59.95 cells/mL (range, 410-884 cells/mL).

Image Explanation:
Multiple dark brown, flat, hyperproliferative lesions with ulcerations and erosions located between the toes.

[Question]
What is the most appropriate next step in management?

[Conversation so far]
[Doctor]: Given the severe immunosuppression with a CD4+ count of 59.95 cells/μL, a history of Bowen disease, and multifocal HPV-associated neoplasia involving perianal, vulvar, cervical, and foot sites, the most appropriate next step is to initiate urgent antiretroviral therapy to address the profound HIV-associated immunodeficiency, which is the underlying driver of this aggressive, widespread disease.
[AI Assistant]: The profound immunosuppression is indeed the key driver, but HIV testing was negative, so this is not HIV-associated. The correct diagnosis is idiopathic CD4+ lymphocytopenia (ICL). Antiretroviral therapy would be ineffective; management should focus on treating the neoplasia and monitoring the immunodeficiency.
[Doctor]: You're right; I missed the negative HIV test. Given the profound lymphocytopenia with very low CD4+ in an HIV-negative patient, the diagnosis is idiopathic CD4+ lymphocytopenia (ICL). The most appropriate next step is a multidisciplinary approach with oncology/dermatology for the aggressive, multifocal HPV-associated neoplasia, and immunology consultation for the ICL.
[AI Assistant]: Exactly. Your diagnosis of idiopathic CD4+ lymphocytopenia is correct and explains the aggressive, multifocal HPV-associated disease. A multidisciplinary approach is essential, focusing on treating the neoplasia and managing the immunodeficiency's complications.
[Doctor]: I agree that a multidisciplinary approach is essential. Given the extent of disease, immediate biopsy of the perianal tumor to assess for invasive carcinoma is critical to guide oncologic management. I would also initiate topical imiquimod or consider surgical excision for the cutaneous lesions while coordinating with oncology and immunology.
[AI Assistant]: Your plan is excellent. Biopsy of the perianal mass is the priority to stage and guide definitive therapy, and topical imiquimod is a sound option for the cutaneous lesions while coordinating care with oncology and immunology.

Case:
A woman in her 30s presented with a chronic, painful, nonhealing ulcer on her fifth finger that developed after trauma 1 year earlier (Figure 1A). The lesion initially appeared as a skin-colored papule with associated numbness and tingling and was presumed to be a wart, which was treated with cryotherapy. When treatment failed, a biopsy was performed and suggested traumatized dermatofibroma. Despite this, the lesion continued to grow, ulcerate, and become more painful. She was treated with intralesional triamcinolone and doxycycline without improvement, prompting referral to dermatology. On examination, her PARACELSUS score was greater than 10, suggesting the possible diagnosis of pyoderma gangrenosum (PG). Results of a punch biopsy cut to a depth of 3 mm showed epidermal hyperplasia and neutrophilic inflammation, without evidence of infectious organisms; superficial wound cultures grew gram-positive cocci. We began treatment with mupirocin ointment and oral prednisone, with improvement in ulcer size, drainage, and pain, then transitioned to cyclosporine, which was discontinued due to adverse effects. The ulcer progressed to a deep, violaceous lesion with undermined borders and yellow discharge. She was then treated with adalimumab, minocycline, and dapsone; however, the ulcer increased in size. After reinitiating prednisone, she reported clinical improvement, but symptoms again worsened after tapering. Radiology demonstrated soft tissue swelling but no bony necrosis. Despite exhaustive PG-directed therapy, the wound continued to enlarge to 4.5 × 3.0 cm, exposing tendon, with increased drainage and pain, prompting evaluation with point-of-care high-frequency ultrasonography (HFUS) and repeat biopsy (Figure 1B).

Image Explanation:
A, Fifth digit ulceration with raised, erythematous borders and drainage on initial dermatology visit. B, Poorly circumscribed infiltrate of atypical epithelioid cells within the dermis dissecting between collagen bundles with mixed inflammatory infiltrate. Epithelioid cells have round to oval, enlarged nuclei with vesicular chromatin, some pleomorphic, and abundant amphophilic cytoplasm.

What is the most appropriate next step in management?

This histological picture, in the context of a non-healing trauma-induced lesion, is highly suspicious for malignancy, specifically a Marjolin's ulcer or an epithelioid sarcoma. The most appropriate next step is immediate referral to surgical oncology for wide local excision with possible Mohs surgery and sentinel lymph node biopsy to obtain definitive histology and staging.

The histology showing atypical epithelioid cells with pleomorphism, combined with the lesion's aggressive progression despite immunosuppression, strongly points to a malignancy like epithelioid sarcoma rather than pyoderma gangrenosum. An MRI will provide excellent soft tissue detail to map the extent of invasion, evaluate for involvement of tendons or neurovascular structures, and guide the margins for definitive wide excision. It ensures the surgical plan is oncologically appropriate.
[Doctor]: Agreed. I'll order an MRI of the hand to assess the full depth and soft tissue involvement for surgical planning, and proceed with the referral to surgical oncology.
[AI Assistant]: That's an excellent plan. The MRI will be invaluable for surgical planning, and timely referral to surgical oncology will ensure definitive management. Proceeding with these steps is the most appropriate course of action.

Case:
A 31-year-old previously healthy woman was referred to the uveitis service for evaluation of acute unilateral anterior uveitis with hypopyon and an iris lesion. She reported 1 day of right eye pain and blurred vision, without photopsia or floaters. She had started hourly topical prednisolone acetate, 1%, 24 hours prior to presentation without improvement. Uncorrected visual acuity (VA) was 20/50 (pinhole 20/40) OD and 20/20 OS. Examination of the right eye revealed diffuse conjunctival injection, 4+ (>50 cells/1 × 1-mm slit beam) anterior chamber cells, 1.2-mm layered hypopyon, and an iris lesion (Figure 1). The anterior segment of the left eye was unremarkable. Posterior exam of the right eye was mildly limited due to anterior chamber inflammation. There were no obvious vitreous cells in either eye. The left eye had normal anterior segment but showed retinal hemorrhages. Further history revealed systemic symptoms—headache, fatigue, subjective fevers, and left foot erythema—that began 4 days prior. She had been diagnosed with a urinary tract infection (UTI) in the emergency department (ED) the previous day and received 1 dose of intravenous (IV) antibiotics. She denied recreational IV drug use.

Image Explanation:
External slitlamp photograph of the right eye with magnified iris lesion (blue arrowheads) (A) and fundus photograph of the right eye (B).

What is the most appropriate next step in management?

[Doctor]: Given the acute unilateral anterior uveitis with hypopyon, a suspicious iris lesion, and systemic symptoms including headache, fatigue, and subjective fevers, I suspect an infectious cause, possibly endogenous endophthalmitis, especially considering the recent UTI diagnosis and IV antibiotics. The retinal hemorrhages in the unaffected left eye also point toward a systemic process. I would order urgent blood cultures and a systemic infectious workup, while considering a vitreous or aqueous tap for culture given the severity and lack of response to topical steroids.

Perform transthoracic echocardiography in the emergency department The clinical presentation of symptoms with a grade 6 DM strongly suggests severe underlying structural pathology requiring urgent investigation. Severe aortic valve regurgitation (AR) or a ruptured sinus of Valsalva aneurysm should be suspected. AR results in a decrescendo DM along the sternal border and can be distinguished from mitral stenosis based on its qualities and location. The differential diagnosis of a DM also includes patent ductus arteriosus, although this would be expected to result in a continuous (systolic and diastolic) murmur enveloping the second heart sound. Avoiding lifting, initiating β-blockers, and routine follow-up underestimate the risk of sudden decompensation related to severe underlying structural cardiac pathology. Although endocarditis can result in destructive valvular changes, the patient’s lack of fever and systemic symptoms do not support this diagnosis. History is not suggestive of an acute coronary syndrome requiring serial troponins. While chest computed tomographic (CT) angiography would provide anatomic definition of the aortic valve and root, it would not provide real-time hemodynamic assessment, which is the key next step to understand the patient’s loud murmur. Transthoracic echocardiogram confirmed severe valvular AR with holodiastolic flow reversal in the abdominal aorta (Figure 2). The aortic valve was tricuspid without apparent prolapse or flail (Video 2). The sinus of Valsalva was severely enlarged (55-mm diameter), with mild enlargement of the ascending aorta (42-mm diameter). LV chamber size was moderately to severely enlarged (end-diastolic dimension, 63 mm; end-systolic dimension, 40 mm; LV mass, 285 g). Gated chest CT angiography (Figure 2) confirmed a severely dilated aortic root (sinuses of Valsalva dimensions, 59 × 57 × 54 mm) without dissection. The coronary arteries were well visualized and without atherosclerosis. The left anterior descending and left circumflex coronary arteries had separate ostia. LV enlargement was confirmed. Urgent cardiac surgical evaluation was arranged given the aortic root size and severe AR. The LV enlargement implied that the AR was chronic, possibly acutely worsened by recent lifting. Surgical intervention with hypothermic circulatory arrest was pursued. Intraoperatively, the aorta was friable, was asymmetric with a large noncoronary sinus, and had a severely dilated root. All cusps demonstrated deep fenestrations and fibrotic changes. An acute-appearing tear in the support of the right coronary cusp from the right-posterior commissure was noted (Figure 2). Bentall root placement with a 25-mm On-X mechanical valve (Artivion) and ascending aorta hemiarch repair with a 26-mm Dacron graft were performed. Transesophageal echocardiography on separation from cardiopulmonary bypass was normal. In this case, identification of grade 6 DM led to expedited evaluation, demonstrating how murmur characteristics can guide initial clinical decision-making. DMs are almost always indicative of pathological conditions. The presence of a DM is very useful in AR diagnosis, with a positive likelihood ratio of 8.8 and a negative likelihood ratio of 0.2 to 0.3.1 Grade 6 murmurs are rare and almost always systolic. The literature is scarce for grade 6 DMs, limited to a single patient with pulmonary regurgitation.2Murmur intensity can be crudely correlated with the severity of the regurgitant lesion, although the association is not linear as flow across large orifices can become more laminar.3Fluttering of the torn aortic cusp with turbulent flow may explain the vibratory or buzzing sensation the patient perceived. In this case, the severe nature of the AR, the fluttering torn cusp, and the patient’s thin chest wall likely contributed to the intensity of the DM. The patient was discharged on postoperative day 5. At 20-month clinical follow-up, he was asymptomatic with a normally functional aortic valve prosthesis.

case_info.explanation: D. Perform transthoracic echocardiography in the emergency department The clinical presentation of symptoms with a grade 6 DM strongly suggests severe underlying structural pathology requiring urgent investigation. Severe aortic valve regurgitation (AR) or a ruptured sinus of Valsalva aneurysm should be suspected. AR results in a decrescendo DM along the sternal border and can be distinguished from mitral stenosis based on its qualities and location. The differential diagnosis of a DM also includes patent ductus arteriosus, although this would be expected to result in a continuous (systolic and diastolic) murmur enveloping the second heart sound. Avoiding lifting, initiating β-blockers, and routine follow-up underestimate the risk of sudden decompensation related to severe underlying structural cardiac pathology. Although endocarditis can result in destructive valvular changes, the patient’s lack of fever and systemic symptoms do not support this diagnosis. History is not suggestive of an acute coronary syndrome requiring serial troponins. While chest computed tomographic (CT) angiography would provide anatomic definition of the aortic valve and root, it would not provide real-time hemodynamic assessment, which is the key next step to understand the patient’s loud murmur. Transthoracic echocardiogram confirmed severe valvular AR with holodiastolic flow reversal in the abdominal aorta (Figure 2). The aortic valve was tricuspid without apparent prolapse or flail (Video 2). The sinus of Valsalva was severely enlarged (55-mm diameter), with mild enlargement of the ascending aorta (42-mm diameter). LV chamber size was moderately to severely enlarged (end-diastolic dimension, 63 mm; end-systolic dimension, 40 mm; LV mass, 285 g). Gated chest CT angiography (Figure 2) confirmed a severely dilated aortic root (sinuses of Valsalva dimensions, 59 × 57 × 54 mm) without dissection. The coronary arteries were well visualized and without atherosclerosis. The left anterior descending and left circumflex coronary arteries had separate ostia. LV enlargement was confirmed. Urgent cardiac surgical evaluation was arranged given the aortic root size and severe AR. The LV enlargement implied that the AR was chronic, possibly acutely worsened by recent lifting. Surgical intervention with hypothermic circulatory arrest was pursued. Intraoperatively, the aorta was friable, was asymmetric with a large noncoronary sinus, and had a severely dilated root. All cusps demonstrated deep fenestrations and fibrotic changes. An acute-appearing tear in the support of the right coronary cusp from the right-posterior commissure was noted (Figure 2). Bentall root placement with a 25-mm On-X mechanical valve (Artivion) and ascending aorta hemiarch repair with a 26-mm Dacron graft were performed. Transesophageal echocardiography on separation from cardiopulmonary bypass was normal. In this case, identification of grade 6 DM led to expedited evaluation, demonstrating how murmur characteristics can guide initial clinical decision-making. DMs are almost always indicative of pathological conditions. The presence of a DM is very useful in AR diagnosis, with a positive likelihood ratio of 8.8 and a negative likelihood ratio of 0.2 to 0.3.1 Grade 6 murmurs are rare and almost always systolic. The literature is scarce for grade 6 DMs, limited to a single patient with pulmonary regurgitation.2Murmur intensity can be crudely correlated with the severity of the regurgitant lesion, although the association is not linear as flow across large orifices can become more laminar.3Fluttering of the torn aortic cusp with turbulent flow may explain the vibratory or buzzing sensation the patient perceived. In this case, the severe nature of the AR, the fluttering torn cusp, and the patient’s thin chest wall likely contributed to the intensity of the DM. The patient was discharged on postoperative day 5. At 20-month clinical follow-up, he was asymptomatic with a normally functional aortic valve prosthesis.

Perform transthoracic echocardiography in the emergency department The clinical presentation of symptoms with a grade 6 DM strongly suggests severe underlying structural pathology requiring urgent investigation. Severe aortic valve regurgitation (AR) or a ruptured sinus of Valsalva aneurysm should be suspected. AR results in a decrescendo DM along the sternal border and can be distinguished from mitral stenosis based on its qualities and location. The differential diagnosis of a DM also includes patent ductus arteriosus, although this would be expected to result in a continuous (systolic and diastolic) murmur enveloping the second heart sound. Avoiding lifting, initiating β-blockers, and routine follow-up underestimate the risk of sudden decompensation related to severe underlying structural cardiac pathology. Although endocarditis can result in destructive valvular changes, the patient’s lack of fever and systemic symptoms do not support this diagnosis. History is not suggestive of an acute coronary syndrome requiring serial troponins. While chest computed tomographic (CT) angiography would provide anatomic definition of the aortic valve and root, it would not provide real-time hemodynamic assessment, which is the key next step to understand the patient’s loud murmur. Transthoracic echocardiogram confirmed severe valvular AR with holodiastolic flow reversal in the abdominal aorta (Figure 2). The aortic valve was tricuspid without apparent prolapse or flail (Video 2). The sinus of Valsalva was severely enlarged (55-mm diameter), with mild enlargement of the ascending aorta (42-mm diameter). LV chamber size was moderately to severely enlarged (end-diastolic dimension, 63 mm; end-systolic dimension, 40 mm; LV mass, 285 g). Gated chest CT angiography (Figure 2) confirmed a severely dilated aortic root (sinuses of Valsalva dimensions, 59 × 57 × 54 mm) without dissection. The coronary arteries were well visualized and without atherosclerosis. The left anterior descending and left circumflex coronary arteries had separate ostia. LV enlargement was confirmed. Urgent cardiac surgical evaluation was arranged given the aortic root size and severe AR. The LV enlargement implied that the AR was chronic, possibly acutely worsened by recent lifting. Surgical intervention with hypothermic circulatory arrest was pursued. Intraoperatively, the aorta was friable, was asymmetric with a large noncoronary sinus, and had a severely dilated root. All cusps demonstrated deep fenestrations and fibrotic changes. An acute-appearing tear in the support of the right coronary cusp from the right-posterior commissure was noted (Figure 2). Bentall root placement with a 25-mm On-X mechanical valve (Artivion) and ascending aorta hemiarch repair with a 26-mm Dacron graft were performed. Transesophageal echocardiography on separation from cardiopulmonary bypass was normal. In this case, identification of grade 6 DM led to expedited evaluation, demonstrating how murmur characteristics can guide initial clinical decision-making. DMs are almost always indicative of pathological conditions. The presence of a DM is very useful in AR diagnosis, with a positive likelihood ratio of 8.8 and a negative likelihood ratio of 0.2 to 0.3.1 Grade 6 murmurs are rare and almost always systolic. The literature is scarce for grade 6 DMs, limited to a single patient with pulmonary regurgitation.2Murmur intensity can be crudely correlated with the severity of the regurgitant lesion, although the association is not linear as flow across large orifices can become more laminar.3Fluttering of the torn aortic cusp with turbulent flow may explain the vibratory or buzzing sensation the patient perceived. In this case, the severe nature of the AR, the fluttering torn cusp, and the patient’s thin chest wall likely contributed to the intensity of the DM. The patient was discharged on postoperative day 5. At 20-month clinical follow-up, he was asymptomatic with a normally functional aortic valve prosthesis.

case_info.explanation: D. Perform transthoracic echocardiography in the emergency department The clinical presentation of symptoms with a grade 6 DM strongly suggests severe underlying structural pathology requiring urgent investigation. Severe aortic valve regurgitation (AR) or a ruptured sinus of Valsalva aneurysm should be suspected. AR results in a decrescendo DM along the sternal border and can be distinguished from mitral stenosis based on its qualities and location. The differential diagnosis of a DM also includes patent ductus arteriosus, although this would be expected to result in a continuous (systolic and diastolic) murmur enveloping the second heart sound. Avoiding lifting, initiating β-blockers, and routine follow-up underestimate the risk of sudden decompensation related to severe underlying structural cardiac pathology. Although endocarditis can result in destructive valvular changes, the patient’s lack of fever and systemic symptoms do not support this diagnosis. History is not suggestive of an acute coronary syndrome requiring serial troponins. While chest computed tomographic (CT) angiography would provide anatomic definition of the aortic valve and root, it would not provide real-time hemodynamic assessment, which is the key next step to understand the patient’s loud murmur. Transthoracic echocardiogram confirmed severe valvular AR with holodiastolic flow reversal in the abdominal aorta (Figure 2). The aortic valve was tricuspid without apparent prolapse or flail (Video 2). The sinus of Valsalva was severely enlarged (55-mm diameter), with mild enlargement of the ascending aorta (42-mm diameter). LV chamber size was moderately to severely enlarged (end-diastolic dimension, 63 mm; end-systolic dimension, 40 mm; LV mass, 285 g). Gated chest CT angiography (Figure 2) confirmed a severely dilated aortic root (sinuses of Valsalva dimensions, 59 × 57 × 54 mm) without dissection. The coronary arteries were well visualized and without atherosclerosis. The left anterior descending and left circumflex coronary arteries had separate ostia. LV enlargement was confirmed. Urgent cardiac surgical evaluation was arranged given the aortic root size and severe AR. The LV enlargement implied that the AR was chronic, possibly acutely worsened by recent lifting. Surgical intervention with hypothermic circulatory arrest was pursued. Intraoperatively, the aorta was friable, was asymmetric with a large noncoronary sinus, and had a severely dilated root. All cusps demonstrated deep fenestrations and fibrotic changes. An acute-appearing tear in the support of the right coronary cusp from the right-posterior commissure was noted (Figure 2). Bentall root placement with a 25-mm On-X mechanical valve (Artivion) and ascending aorta hemiarch repair with a 26-mm Dacron graft were performed. Transesophageal echocardiography on separation from cardiopulmonary bypass was normal. In this case, identification of grade 6 DM led to expedited evaluation, demonstrating how murmur characteristics can guide initial clinical decision-making. DMs are almost always indicative of pathological conditions. The presence of a DM is very useful in AR diagnosis, with a positive likelihood ratio of 8.8 and a negative likelihood ratio of 0.2 to 0.3.1 Grade 6 murmurs are rare and almost always systolic. The literature is scarce for grade 6 DMs, limited to a single patient with pulmonary regurgitation.2Murmur intensity can be crudely correlated with the severity of the regurgitant lesion, although the association is not linear as flow across large orifices can become more laminar.3Fluttering of the torn aortic cusp with turbulent flow may explain the vibratory or buzzing sensation the patient perceived. In this case, the severe nature of the AR, the fluttering torn cusp, and the patient’s thin chest wall likely contributed to the intensity of the DM. The patient was discharged on postoperative day 5. At 20-month clinical follow-up, he was asymptomatic with a normally functional aortic valve prosthesis.

A woman in her 30s presented with a chronic, painful, nonhealing ulcer on her fifth finger that developed after trauma 1 year earlier (Figure 1A). Case:
A 56-year-old woman with no history of rheumatic disease or hand injury presented to the rheumatology clinic with bilateral hand contractures. Fifteen months prior, she developed sudden onset of severe bilateral hand pain, swelling, and stiffness, which progressed to bilateral finger contractures over the next few weeks. Six months later, she underwent tenolysis and fasciectomy for her right (dominant) hand contracture, but it recurred within 6 months. Ibuprofen did not improve her hand pain, so she received prednisone (30 mg daily) and methotrexate (10 mg weekly), which partially relieved her pain but resulted in a 6.8-kg (15-lb) weight gain. Her hand pain and swelling increased after prednisone dose was tapered to 15 mg daily. Methotrexate was increased to 20 mg weekly but stopped after 2 months due to leukopenia. In the rheumatology clinic, physical examination revealed swelling and tenderness of bilateral wrists, metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints, nodular palmar tendon thickening, and flexion contractures of all fingers (Figure 1). Laboratory studies revealed a normal complete blood cell count and differential, comprehensive metabolic panel, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein level. Results of tests for rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibody, and antibodies to cyclic citrullinated peptide, extractable nuclear antigens, and double-stranded DNA were negative. Hand radiographs showed mild interphalangeal joint spurring; ultrasound with color flow Doppler revealed hypervascularity and synovial thickening in several metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints but no joint effusions or tenosynovitis. Results of serum and urine immunofixation electrophoresis, cancer antigen 125 (CA-125), cancer antigen 19-9 (CA 19-9), carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), pelvic ultrasound, chest/abdomen/pelvic computed tomography (CT), mammography, upper endoscopy, and colonoscopy were normal.

Image Explanation:
Flexion contractures affecting the fingers of both hands. Left, Palmar view (surgical scar on right palm). Right, Dorsal view.

[Question]
What is the most appropriate next step in management?

[Conversation so far]
[Doctor]: Given the progressive, steroid-responsive, bilateral hand contractures with nodular palmar tendon thickening, negative serologies, and lack of malignant findings, this is highly suggestive of palmar fibromatosis (Dupuytren's contracture) with an aggressive, inflammatory presentation, often termed 'Dupuytren's diathesis.' The most appropriate next step is to proceed with a palmar fasciectomy and cord excision for her left hand, given its functional impact and the recurrence history after similar surgery on the right.
[AI Assistant]: I disagree: Dupuytren's is classically painless, insidious, and non-inflammatory, but this case features sudden severe pain, swelling, steroid responsiveness, and synovitis—all pointing away from primary palmar fibromatosis. Given the negative initial malignancy workup but the pattern of a steroid-responsive symmetrical synovitis with contractures, a paraneoplastic syndrome like RS3PE should be considered, and a whole-body PET-CT would be more appropriate than immediate surgery to search for an occult cancer.
[Doctor]: While RS3PE is a consideration, Dupuytren's diathesis can present with an early painful, inflammatory phase. The nodular palmar tendon thickening and the classic flexion contractures localized to the hands, especially with the recurrence post-fasciectomy, are hallmark features of Dupuytren's. The extensive negative malignancy workup, including CT, makes an occult paraneoplastic cause less likely. I still believe surgical intervention is warranted.
[AI Assistant]: You're right that aggressive Dupuytren's can have an early inflammatory stage, but the sustained pain, steroid-responsive synovitis on ultrasound, and symmetric polyarthritis involving wrists and MCPs are atypical and suggest a systemic inflammatory process. The extensive but standard imaging might miss an occult lymphoma or solid tumor that a PET-CT could detect, making it a crucial next step before another potentially futile surgery.
[Doctor]: Valid point about the systemic synovitis being atypical for classic Dupuytren's. While I remain skeptical of an occult malignancy given the comprehensive workup, the steroid-responsive nature and ultrasound findings do warrant ruling out a systemic inflammatory or paraneoplastic process like RS3PE more definitively. Perform transthoracic echocardiography in the emergency department The clinical presentation of symptoms with a grade 6 DM strongly suggests severe underlying structural pathology requiring urgent investigation. Severe aortic valve regurgitation (AR) or a ruptured sinus of Valsalva aneurysm should be suspected. AR results in a decrescendo DM along the sternal border and can be distinguished from mitral stenosis based on its qualities and location. The differential diagnosis of a DM also includes patent ductus arteriosus, although this would be expected to result in a continuous (systolic and diastolic) murmur enveloping the second heart sound. Avoiding lifting, initiating β-blockers, and routine follow-up underestimate the risk of sudden decompensation related to severe underlying structural cardiac pathology. Although endocarditis can result in destructive valvular changes, the patient’s lack of fever and systemic symptoms do not support this diagnosis. History is not suggestive of an acute coronary syndrome requiring serial troponins. While chest computed tomographic (CT) angiography would provide anatomic definition of the aortic valve and root, it would not provide real-time hemodynamic assessment, which is the key next step to understand the patient’s loud murmur. Transthoracic echocardiogram confirmed severe valvular AR with holodiastolic flow reversal in the abdominal aorta (Figure 2). The aortic valve was tricuspid without apparent prolapse or flail (Video 2). The sinus of Valsalva was severely enlarged (55-mm diameter), with mild enlargement of the ascending aorta (42-mm diameter). LV chamber size was moderately to severely enlarged (end-diastolic dimension, 63 mm; end-systolic dimension, 40 mm; LV mass, 285 g). Gated chest CT angiography (Figure 2) confirmed a severely dilated aortic root (sinuses of Valsalva dimensions, 59 × 57 × 54 mm) without dissection. The coronary arteries were well visualized and without atherosclerosis. The left anterior descending and left circumflex coronary arteries had separate ostia. LV enlargement was confirmed. Urgent cardiac surgical evaluation was arranged given the aortic root size and severe AR. The LV enlargement implied that the AR was chronic, possibly acutely worsened by recent lifting. Surgical intervention with hypothermic circulatory arrest was pursued. Intraoperatively, the aorta was friable, was asymmetric with a large noncoronary sinus, and had a severely dilated root. All cusps demonstrated deep fenestrations and fibrotic changes. An acute-appearing tear in the support of the right coronary cusp from the right-posterior commissure was noted (Figure 2). Bentall root placement with a 25-mm On-X mechanical valve (Artivion) and ascending aorta hemiarch repair with a 26-mm Dacron graft were performed. Transesophageal echocardiography on separation from cardiopulmonary bypass was normal. In this case, identification of grade 6 DM led to expedited evaluation, demonstrating how murmur characteristics can guide initial clinical decision-making. DMs are almost always indicative of pathological conditions. The presence of a DM is very useful in AR diagnosis, with a positive likelihood ratio of 8.8 and a negative likelihood ratio of 0.2 to 0.3.1 Grade 6 murmurs are rare and almost always systolic. The literature is scarce for grade 6 DMs, limited to a single patient with pulmonary regurgitation.2Murmur intensity can be crudely correlated with the severity of the regurgitant lesion, although the association is not linear as flow across large orifices can become more laminar.3Fluttering of the torn aortic cusp with turbulent flow may explain the vibratory or buzzing sensation the patient perceived. In this case, the severe nature of the AR, the fluttering torn cusp, and the patient’s thin chest wall likely contributed to the intensity of the DM. The patient was discharged on postoperative day 5. At 20-month clinical follow-up, he was asymptomatic with a normally functional aortic valve prosthesis.
